definition: Authoritative means commanding trust and deference as expert, accurate, and reliable.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word authoritative. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know authoritative should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Field guides come and go, but Merrick's remains the authoritative one: when two rangers disagree about a track, someone reaches for 'the Merrick' and the argument ends.
Credible is milder than authoritative: a credible report clears the bar of belief, while an authoritative one commands deference — others cite it and build on it.
Definitive goes further than authoritative: several authoritative accounts can share a shelf, each trusted and weighty, but the definitive one is the last word, after which the debate closes.

Definitive means the question is settled: the last word, after which debate stops. Authoritative is about weight rather than finality — an authoritative account commands trust, and several can stand on the same shelf; only one can be definitive.

Expert points at the credentials of the person — an expert opinion comes from mastery. Authoritative describes how the account itself is received: others defer to it and build on it, whoever wrote it.

Two accounts of the mine disaster appeared within a year.

A journalist's version sold better, but the inspector's report became the authoritative account: she had descended the shaft herself, logged every timber and valve, and taken sworn statements from all forty-one survivors.
Courts cited her; eventually, the journalist cited her too.
Authoritative marks the version others defer to and build on, because expertise and evidence stand behind it.
Note what it does not mean: the inspector held power over no one.
An authoritative voice is obeyed the way a good map is obeyed — willingly, because doubting it costs more than trusting it.
measured / evaluative, approving
Authoritative praises a source: expert, weighty, deferred to.
Do not let it shade into authoritarian, which condemns a ruler — the two share a root and almost nothing else in tone.
An authoritative editor is trusted; an authoritarian one is merely obeyed.
And age alone earns neither word: a first edition is only the earliest, not the one others defer to.

When the mountain began venting in March, rumor moved faster than ash: school groups repeated one evacuation map, radio hosts another.
Within a week, everyone had settled on a single source.
The observatory's morning bulletin became the authoritative account of the eruption — not by decree, but by use.
Mayors quoted it at press conferences; airlines planned around it; even the scientists' rivals at the university cited its figures before disputing its forecasts.
The bulletin was not the last word on anything.
It revised itself constantly, sometimes hourly, and said so plainly.
Its standing came from somewhere simpler: whenever two claims about the mountain collided, it was the bulletin people checked — and the argument moved on from there.
